episodes.title: Why has gold got so expensive?
episodes.intro: Many of us own jewellery or other items that are gold coloured, but do you own anything that is made from real gold? Gold is a precious metal, which means that there is a limited supply in the world. This not only makes it expensive, but also means that it holds a relatively stable value. So, why are investors interested in it, and should the rest of us start buying more of it? Georgie and Phil discuss this and teach you some new vocabulary.
episodes.question: How much gold has been extracted from the earth over its history?
vocab: something of financial value that can be sold for money
something or somewhere protected from harm or loss
ancient study combining elements of chemistry and mysticism, which attempted to do impossible things like transforming ordinary metals into gold

episodes.title: Are people drinking less alcohol?
episodes.intro: In recent generations many people have chosen to stop drinking alcohol. Surveys from the UK suggest that 16 to 24-year-olds are more likely to be non-drinkers than the older generations. Many people are sharing their experience of drinking less alcohol or being completely sober on social media. Some people have been saying that they want to go out more to drink and have fun with friends, but they have concerns about fitness and wellness. Georgie and Neil discuss this and teach you some new vocabulary.
episodes.question: Many people in the UK and other countries choose to give up alcohol in the new year for the whole of the month of January, but what is the challenge called?
vocab: not drinking alcohol or taking recreational drugs
feeling that you should do something because lots of other people expect you to

praise something or talk about it a lot to get others to try it
strong criticism of a trend; people doing the opposite of a trend

episodes.title: Why does heartbreak hurt so much?
episodes.intro: Anyone who has had their heart broken will know how horrible it feels. But did you know that the pain you feel is not just imaginary – it registers in the same part of the brain that processes physical pain. So, why do we feel this pain? And if it feels so bad, what is the point of being in love in the first place? Neil and Georgie discuss this and teach you some new vocabulary.
episodes.question: Which theory, developed by psychologists in the 1950s, describes a link between children's early bonds with their parents and their romantic relationships as adults?
vocab: feeling of intense, painful sadness after the end of a relationship
unable to cut a connection with someone or something because you depend on it or want more of it all the time
focused on someone, so that you think about them before others
close relationships between family, friends and romantic partners
length of time you will live
